title: What to Eat in Crete: Traditional Dishes Worth Ordering
seoTitle: What to Eat in Crete: 9 Traditional Cretan Dishes to Try
seoDescription: Dakos, gamopilafo, antikristo, staka, kalitsounia, sfakian pie and raki - what each dish actually is, and where in Crete you will find it done properly.
summary: The dishes worth ordering in Crete are dakos (a barley rusk with grated tomato, olive oil and mizithra cheese), gamopilafo (rice cooked in lamb or goat broth, served at weddings), antikristo (lamb slow-roasted upright around an open fire), staka (a rich cooked sheep's-milk cream from western Crete), slow-cooked lamb or goat with wild herbs, kalitsounia (small hand-made cheese or greens pies), the island's sheep and goat cheeses, and sfakian pie with honey. Every meal ends with raki, also called tsikoudia, which is poured for you rather than ordered. None of this is refined cooking: Cretan food is built on a handful of very good local ingredients and long, unhurried cooking, and it is eaten in village tavernas and at family tables rather than in restaurants that plate things elegantly.
body:
Cretan food is memorable because it is honest, not because it is clever. It is tied to everyday life - to family tables and to slow lunches that turn into long conversations - and most of it is cooked the way it has been for decades. Meals are not rushed, food is shared, and guests are treated as part of the family. If you want to understand the island beyond its beaches and landmarks, you have to eat.

The full list of [things to do in Crete](/en/guides/authentic-crete-experiences) is the companion to this page.

Below are the dishes and products locals genuinely eat, with what each one is and where you are most likely to find it done properly.

## The dishes at a glance

| Dish | What it is | Where to try it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dakos | Barley rusk topped with grated ripe tomato, olive oil, oregano and mizithra or xinomizithra | Everywhere - tavernas, seaside cafes, mountain villages, home tables |
| Gamopilafo | Rice slowly cooked in rich lamb or goat broth, finished with lemon and butter or staka | Weddings, baptisms and family celebrations; some traditional tavernas cook it to order |
| Antikristo | Lamb salted and slow-roasted on wooden spits set opposite an open fire | Mountain villages, especially in the shepherding areas of southern and western Crete |
| Staka | Sheep's-milk cream cooked down into a rich, indulgent spread or sauce | Western Crete - served with eggs, or stirred through gamopilafo |
| Lamb or goat with herbs | Free-range meat cooked slowly with olive oil, wild herbs and sometimes lemon | Village tavernas across the mountainous interior |
| Kalitsounia | Small hand-made pies filled with fresh cheese and herbs, or wild greens; sweet versions come with honey | Home kitchens and village bakeries, especially around holidays |
| Cretan cheese | Graviera, mizithra, xinomizithra and anthotyro, mostly from sheep's and goat's milk | Every table; many families still make their own |
| Sfakian pie | Thin pan-cooked pie filled with soft local cheese and drizzled with honey | Sfakia, in southern Crete, and tavernas across the south-west |
| Raki (tsikoudia) | Clear grape-pomace spirit, poured after a meal without being ordered | Any taverna, at the end of any meal |

## Dakos - the plate locals eat without thinking

Dakos is the most honest thing on a Cretan menu. Nobody here describes it as special; they simply eat it, which tells you everything. It starts with a barley rusk - something Cretans have always relied on because it keeps well and fills you up. On top go grated ripe tomatoes, plenty of local olive oil, a little oregano, and soft white cheese: mizithra or xinomizithra.

The magic is not the recipe but the ingredients. Tomatoes that taste like tomatoes. Olive oil that smells like freshly cut grass. Cheese made nearby, often that morning.

## Gamopilafo - the dish cooked for important days

Gamopilafo is not a Tuesday dish. It is food for weddings, baptisms and big family gatherings, and the name says as much: *gamos* means wedding.

At its core it is rice slowly cooked in rich lamb or goat broth. Simple on paper, hard to get right. The rice has to be creamy, the broth deeply flavoured, and it is finished with lemon and either butter or staka. Eating gamopilafo is eating hospitality - this is the plate served to honour guests.

## Antikristo - lamb, salt, fire and time

In the mountains, lamb is slow-roasted on wooden spits arranged around an open fire, the meat facing the flames rather than sitting over them. There are no marinades and no sauces: lamb, coarse salt, fire and time. The result is tender, juicy and lightly smoky, and the cooking method exists to let the meat taste like itself.

## Staka - the island's best-kept secret

Most visitors have never heard of staka, which is part of why it is worth ordering. It is made from sheep's-milk cream cooked slowly until it turns rich and almost indulgent. It belongs to western Crete, and it usually turns up either as eggs with staka or stirred into gamopilafo. It is not light food and does not pretend to be. If you see it on a menu, order it - you may not get another chance.

## Lamb and goat with herbs - food shaped by the land

Crete is mountainous, and the food shows it. Sheep and goats graze freely on wild thyme and oregano, which is why the meat tastes stronger, cleaner and more aromatic here than it does elsewhere. Traditional lamb and goat dishes are cooked slowly with olive oil, herbs and perhaps a little lemon. No heavy sauces, no additions for their own sake.

## Kalitsounia - small pies made by hand

Kalitsounia vary by region and by family. Some are filled with fresh cheese and herbs, some with wild greens, and sweet versions are finished with honey. They are not a factory snack: they are made at home, particularly for holidays, and offered to guests still warm as a sign of welcome.

## Cretan cheese - part of daily life

Cheese is everywhere in Crete, not as a course but as part of ordinary meals. Graviera, mizithra, xinomizithra and anthotyro each have their place, most are made from sheep's and goat's milk, and many families still produce their own. Cheese is eaten with bread, with tomatoes, with honey, or on its own.

## Sfakian pie - sweet and salty, in the right proportion

Sfakian pie comes from Sfakia, in the south. It is thin, cooked in a pan, filled with soft local cheese and drizzled with honey. Salty cheese, warm dough, sweet honey - simple, and quietly addictive. Locals eat it after a meal or on its own.

## Raki - a way of saying you are welcome

Raki, also called tsikoudia, is not really a drink. It is a gesture. After a meal a small glass appears on the table, usually without being asked for, sometimes with fruit or a sweet. What matters is the moment: raki is about conversation and hospitality, and locals sip it slowly. Refusing it can feel faintly impolite, because offering it is how you are told you are welcome.

## What the food tells you

Cretan food is not about trends or presentation. It is about seasonality, simplicity and sharing. These dishes exist because they work and because they bring people together, and tasting them teaches you more about how the island lives than any landmark will.

Gamopilafo, rice cooked in lamb or goat broth, served at weddings and baptisms

faqs.q: What is the most traditional Cretan dish?
faqs.a: Dakos is the most everyday and the most characteristic: a barley rusk topped with grated ripe tomato, local olive oil, oregano and soft mizithra or xinomizithra cheese. Gamopilafo is the most ceremonial - rice cooked in lamb or goat broth, made for weddings and baptisms.

faqs.q: What is staka and where can I find it?
faqs.a: Staka is sheep's-milk cream cooked slowly into a rich spread or sauce. It belongs mainly to western Crete and usually appears as eggs with staka, or stirred through gamopilafo. It is rarely on menus outside the region, so order it when you see it.

faqs.q: What is the difference between raki and ouzo?
faqs.a: Raki, known in Crete as tsikoudia, is distilled from grape pomace and has no aniseed in it, so it is clear and stays clear with water. Ouzo is flavoured with aniseed and turns cloudy. In Crete raki is brought to the table at the end of a meal as a gesture of hospitality, usually without charge.

faqs.q: Is Cretan food good for vegetarians?
faqs.a: Yes. Dakos, kalitsounia with wild greens, the island's cheeses, boiled horta (wild greens), bean dishes and vegetable stews are all standard taverna food, and the Cretan diet leans heavily on vegetables, pulses, grains and olive oil. The celebrated dishes are mostly lamb and goat, but the everyday ones are not.

Lamb salted and roasted slowly on wooden spits arranged upright around an open fire, so the meat cooks facing the flames rather than over them. There is no marinade and no sauce. It is a mountain and shepherding tradition, and it takes hours.
